title: Bucatini Cacio e Pepe
subtitle: Pecorino, black pepper, and starchy pasta water
description: Four ingredients, and all of the difficulty is in the last ninety seconds. The sauce comes together off the heat; the starchy water is what keeps the cheese from seizing into strings.

source.name: Serious Eats
source.author: J. Kenji López-Alt
source.note: Adapted — cooked in a smaller volume of water for a starchier result.

ingredients.raw: 3 ounces (85g) Pecorino Romano, very finely grated, plus more for serving
1 to 2 tablespoons black peppercorns, coarsely cracked
Kosher salt, for the pasta water

steps.text: Bring {{2 quart}} of water to a boil in a large skillet or sauté pan. Salt it lightly — about half of what you'd normally use, since the sauce leans hard on Pecorino. Using less water than a stockpot gives you a starchier cooking liquid, which is the whole trick.
Meanwhile, toast the cracked peppercorns in a dry skillet over medium heat until fragrant, about 1 minute. Tip them into a small bowl and set aside.
Add the bucatini to the boiling water and cook, stirring often, until just shy of al dente — about 2 minutes less than the package says. It will finish cooking in the sauce.
Reserve {{1.5 cup}} of the pasta water, then drain. Return the empty pan to low heat, add the butter and toasted pepper, and swirl until the butter melts and foams.
Add the pasta and {{0.5 cup}} of the reserved water. Toss vigorously for about 30 seconds, until the liquid thickens and clings.

Take the pan off the heat and wait 30 seconds — this matters. Add the Pecorino in three additions, tossing hard between each and loosening with splashes of pasta water. Cheese added to a pan that's too hot will break into strings instead of melting into sauce.
Serve immediately, with more Pecorino and pepper at the table. It does not wait.

notes: Grate the Pecorino on a Microplane. Coarsely grated cheese is the single most common cause of a broken sauce.
If it does break, pull the pan off the heat, add a splash of cold pasta water, and toss hard. It usually comes back.
Crack the peppercorns in a mortar or under a heavy pan — a grinder makes dust, and you want actual pieces.
